title: Raga Jaijavanti
hook: where the Granth's ragas end, one voice sings alone: Guru Tegh Bahadur, and a kingdom built like a wall of sand

segments.voice: Yesterday, a hymn in Prabhati, Kabir's song of one light and one clay. Your line was light at dawn. Who did you picture under the same morning light? Day one thousand one hundred twenty-six.

A sandcastle at the edge of the tide can be a fine thing. Towers, a moat, a wall patted smooth with both hands. Everyone on the beach knows how the story ends, and still somebody builds it, and still it's worth a photo. In the Guru Granth Sahib, the long run of ragas has been carrying us page by page, from evening to dawn and back. Today we reach the place where the ragas end. The section is called Jaijavanti, it holds a single voice, and in its first hymn there's a wall made of sand. Today: Raga Jaijavanti.
screen: `A WALL PATTED SMOOTH WITH BOTH HANDS.` → `WHERE THE RAGAS END.` → `ONE VOICE, AND A WALL OF SAND.`

segments.voice: Where we are: Jaijavanti follows Prabhati, and it is the last of the raga sections in the Granth's order. After it come verses gathered without a raga heading, and at the very end a page we'll open in two days. Jaijavanti is short, and every hymn in it is by Guru Tegh Bahadur. Tradition says his hymns were added to the Granth by his son, Guru Gobind Singh. In many ragas, voices take turns: Gurus, then Bhagats. Here, one voice sings alone, the way a concert sometimes ends with a single singer. Now the first hymn. It opens with a doubled call, in paraphrase: remember the Lord, remember the Lord; this alone is your work. Leave clinging to Maya, the world's glitter, and take shelter with God. Count the world's pleasures as false; the whole show is false. Then two pictures. Wealth, he says, is like riches in a dream. And the rule of the whole earth is like a wall of sand. Listen to how gently that's put. The hymn doesn't sneer at wealth or power. A dream can be vivid. A sand wall can be well made. The point is only what they're made of, and how long they stand. Put against that, one thing is named as your work: remembering. Not owning more, not ruling more. Remembering the One, twice over, so you hear it. After all the moods, morning and evening, spring and rain, the last raga sets down a plain instruction. Tomorrow, the same voice speaks about time. Today's line: the last raga.
screen: `AFTER PRABHATI, THE RAGAS END.` · `ONE VOICE: GURU TEGH BAHADUR.` · `REMEMBER, REMEMBER: YOUR WORK.` · `A KINGDOM LIKE A WALL OF SAND.` · then, large: `THE LAST RAGA.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: listen to Jaijavanti, and set one thing down beside the sand. If you can, play a shabad of Guru Tegh Bahadur sung in Raga Jaijavanti. If not, sit in the quiet. Bring to mind one thing you've been building lately: a savings goal, a reputation, a project. No judgment; it may be good work. Just notice what it's made of. Then let it rest, the way you'd leave a sandcastle on the beach, and turn to the breath. Stay with it, plainly, as if remembering were the only job you had for these two minutes. If you pray, you can let Guru Tegh Bahadur's doubled call, remember the Lord, sit on the breath. If you don't, simply come back to breathing each time the building starts again. The bell holds the time.
Raga Jaijavanti. The last raga section of the Granth, holding hymns of Guru Tegh Bahadur alone, which opens: remember the Lord, remember; this alone is your work. Today's word.
Your line: the last raga. Once today, when you're adding to something you're building, pause for one breath and remember what it's made of. Day one thousand one hundred twenty-six.

howItsDone: Guru Tegh Bahadur's hymns in Raga Jaijavanti are sung in kirtan, and Sikh tradition remembers him as the Guru who gave his life for others' freedom of faith.
